This paper serves as the companion paper for the authors' multi-objective optimization suite. 

The reviewers were very positive on the work. They mentioned the strong motivation for the benchmark, the clear writing, and informative case studies and experiments. 

After reading through the discussions, I agree with reviewers about the high quality of this work, and the high potential for impact. I recommend acceptance.

We sincerely thank the reviewers and ACs for their time and effort. Given the length of our rebuttal, we summarize the key points below, beginning with the strengths of LibMOON:

**Recognized strengths of LibMOON**  
- **A timely library**: All reviewers agree that the problem of gradient-based multiobjective optimization (MOO) is highly important. The introduction of LibMOON is **timely**, as previous libraries focus on evolutionary computation. With the growing trend of **large-scale** machine learning problems, a gradient-based MOO library is necessary due to its superior scalability compared to evolutionary approaches.
  
- **Importance of MOO**: MOO, though critical, has been somewhat overlooked in past work. Many real-world problems, such as balancing fairness and accuracy in trustworthy machine learning or safety and performance trade-offs, are inherently multiobjective. LibMOON provides the first standardized framework for studying these problems.

We then summarize the improvements made in the rebuttal in response to the reviewers.

**Improvement during rebuttal**
- **Documentation and Index of LibMOON**: Following the reviewers' suggestions, we have improved LibMOON's documentation, which is now well-organized using Sphinx and available [here](https://libmoondocs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). The index can be accessed [here](https://github.com/xzhang2523/libmoon). The document has five sections: "Getting Started," "User Guide," "Developer Guide," "API Reference," and "Gallery." New problems, methods, or architectures can be easily integrated into LibMOON using the standard APIs and guidings. 
- **Experimental results**: We enhanced the report by providing a detailed analysis of the mean and standard deviation of results, examining why some methods show large deviations while others are more deterministic. This technical report aids practitioners in selecting the appropriate MOO method.
- **Flexibility and Community of LibMOON Maintenance**: We provide detailed examples of adding new methods, problems, or architectures to LibMOON. For instance, the recently published LoRA-PSL (Chen et al., 2024) can be integrated with minimal code. Additionally, there is a [request](https://github.com/xzhang2523/libmoon/issues/4) to collaborate on incorporating a new architecture (Tuan et al., 2024). LibMOON offers IM, WeChat, and Slack groups for user feedback.
- **GPU Acceleration**: We present an analysis and numerical results on the extent of GPU acceleration in LibMOON.

The reviewer feedback is as follows:

- Reviewer vVnF gave a positive score of 7 after we clarified a misunderstanding regarding the scope.
- Reviewer jTTe gave the lowest score of 4; we hope our detailed response will address his concerns.
- Reviewers PsFx and f2ft consistently gave positive scores of 7 and 6, respectively.


---
Reference

[1] Chen et al. Efficient Pareto Manifold Learning with Low-Rank Structure. ICML 2024. 

[2] Tuan et al. A Hyper-Transformer model for Controllable Pareto Front Learning with Split Feasibility Constraints. Neural Networks. 2024.

We deeply thank you for your thorough reviews and positive feedback. We hope our response addresses your concerns.

> **Q1. The overview page of LibMOON is missing.** 

It is now fixed in the [documentation](https://libmoondocs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/guide/Framework.html).

> **Q2. Relationship with BoTorch.** 

Thank you for your valuable suggestion. Currently, there are relatively few learning-based/decomposition based multiobjective Baysian optimization (MOBO) hat are not included in BoTorch. We view these methods as extensions of Pareto set learning (PSL). 
We initially implemented MOBO methods from scratch just for flexibility. We fully agree with your suggestion to interface these methods with [BoTorch](https://botorch.org/) or [HEBO](https://github.com/huawei-noah/HEBO). In fact, we are already planning to implement this in future versions.

> **Q3. Backend-agnostic implementation so that at least the benchmark problems.** 

Thank you for your advice. Indeed, a backend-agnostic (JAX, TF, PyTorch...) or platform-agnostic (C++, python, R...) implement of LibMOON is valuable but outside our current scope. Currently, LibMOON focuses on academic use and our main effort focus on including well-known/published gradient-based MOO methods. We will consider your suggestion and industrial impact for future work.

> **C1. Writing clarity.** 

Thanks for your thorough review. Those code snippets are called "listings" because we use the LaTeX listing environment (https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Code_listing). We'll clarify them and adjust font size and caption placement in the revised paper.

In response to the ease or difficulty of adding new methods or architectures, we provide an example of how to integrate a new model architecture, specifically the low-rank adaptation model (Chen et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024), into LibMOON. Detailed instructions for adding new architectures can also be found [here](https://libmoondocs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/develop/custom_architecture.html).

LoRA PSL aims to optimize the following objective function:

$$\min\_{x_0, \mathbf{A}_1, \dots, \mathbf{A}_m, \mathbf{B}_1, \dots, \mathbf{B}_m} \mathbb{E}\_{\lambda} \left[ \sum\_{i=1}^{m} \lambda_i f_i\left(x_0 + \sum\_{j=1}^m \lambda_j \mathbf{A}_j \mathbf{B}_j; \lambda\right) \right].$$

LoRA-PSL and PSL both aim to optimize an expectation over the entire preference space to identify models that produce Pareto-optimal solutions. However, LoRA-PSL is distinct in its use of a low-rank adaptation strategy, which reduces the number of parameters. 

**For visual results on synthetic and multitask learning problems, see the attached PDF**
---
Reference

[1] Chen et al. Efficient Pareto Manifold Learning with Low-Rank Structure. ICML. 2024.

[2] Zhong et al. Panacea: Pareto Alignment via Preference Adaptation for LLMs. ArXiv. 2024.

Thank you for finding our library useful. We followed your instructions on writing directly and hope our response addresses your other concerns. 

> **W1.** No illustration related to the use of large-scale models with millions of parameters whereas the scalability is emphasized in the abstract as the motivation of this paper.

We illustrate the application to large-scale models through the multi-MNIST problem, which involves a hypernetwork. 
This hypernetwork takes preference vectors $\lambda$ as input, outpus the target network parameters, and in total has 3,243,410 (~3M) parameters, while the target network solely has 31,910 parameters.

> **W2.** Pure multi-objective learning problems are not included (whereas multi-task learning problems are included in the explanations in Fig. 1). 

We beg to argue we have incorporated multiple "pure multiobjective learning problems" into LibMOON. In Section 5.2, for example, we mentioned ZDT1, and many other standard MOPs are included. We would appreciate it if you could suggest more related "pure multiobjective learning problems".

> **W3.** There is no discussion about how to evaluate the trained Pareto set models.

After obtaining the Pareto set models, we generate uniform preference angle grids in $[0, \frac{\pi}{2}]^{m-1}$, convert them to preference vectors, input these vectors into the Pareto set model, and evaluate the performance of the resulting solutions.
We will add the discussion to the next revision in Appendix B.2.

> **W5.** A test problem used in computational experiments looks too simple. **I3.** Line 280: "We use ZDT1 to illustrate the different behaviors of Pareto set learning (PSL) methods". It seems that "ZDT1" is too simple for compare "Pareto Set Learning" methods. Fig. 4 simply explain the characteristic features of each scalarizing function.

Since W5 and I3 are related, we combine them together. ZDT1 is used as an illustrative example. 
Additionally, we include a multitask learning problem using Pareto set learning in the appendix. 

> **I1.** Line 27: "In non-degenerate problems, no single solution can attain the minimum of all objectives simultaneously." In the EMO community, "degenerate problems" usually mean that the dimensionality of the Pareto front of an m-objective degenerate problem is less than (m - 1). Even in this case, no single solution can attain the minimum of all objectives simultaneously. Thus, it seems that this sentence may need some modifications.


Many thanks for your suggestion. We will revise it to "non-trivial problems" or "for general multiobjective optimization."

We thank you for your kind and detailed review of our work. We hope that our following response can address your concerns. 

**I1**. i)  How easy/hard it is to add new methods or architectures? ii)  How flexible is the code to add other solutions. iii)  The willingness/planning for the authors to keep the library activate and updated. As of now, it feels more like a black-box collection of static methods and benchmarks. iv)  How the code has been designed and implemented? 
**L1.** open-endedness, flexibility, API extensions, etc.

We answer the problem how code is designed and implemented here, and for other questions, please refer to our general response 1. 

LibMOON consists of three main classes: the problem class, the solver class, and the architecture class.

- **Problem Class:** Focuses on reimplementing the evaluation function, with support for synthetic and multitask learning problems.
  
- **Solver Class:** As detailed in our main paper, the objective function for both aggregation and gradient modifier methods can be expressed as optimizing a **generalized aggregation function** with adaptive or fixed weights. The primary task for each MOO method is to design a specific class (e.g., CoreMGDA, CoreEPO, ...) that outputs these dynamic weights, allowing for high modularity. This property also applies to Pareto set learning.

- **Architecture Class:** This class to design network structure such as hypernetwork model is decoupled from the problem and solver classes, allowing for independent design.

To design a new problem/method/architecture, please refer to our [tutorial](https://libmoondocs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/develop/add_method.html). 



**I2.** What is reported as MTL problems are far from the typical settings tested in gradient-conflict MTL approaches (e.g., multi-MNIST, multi-classification in CelebA, NYUv2, Cityscapes, etc.). 

LibMOON is intentionally not designed to address such MTL problems. 
Recent studies suggest that for models with strong capacity (e.g., deep ResNet), traditional gradient-conflict MTL methods may not effectively solve multi-task learning tasks like CelebA, NYUc2, and Cityscapes (Xin et al. 2022, Hu et al 2023, Lin et al 2022). These methods aim to **find a single solution that benefits all objectives**, whereas LibMOON focuses on studying the distribution of solutions on the Pareto set/front and learning the entire Pareto front. Since there is no clear evidence that large problems like CelebA, NYUc2, and Cityscapes have a Pareto front, these tasks are excluded from LibMOON's scope.

> **R1** I think the paper falls quite short when it comes to MTL. 

> **R2** mention the possibility of optimizing the last-common representation of the network

We appreciate the precious insights of the reviewer on MTL. We will accordingly elaborate the relation between our library and MTL in a new section in the appendix.

> **I3.** The empirical results do not serve much of a purpose in the current state of the manuscript, beyond assessing that the code works. It is a necessary sanity check, but I am not sure if they add much to the current paper.

Thanks for your advice. We consider the empirical results could either remain in the main paper or be moved to the appendix, as shown in past examples like the NeurIPS DB paper (Liao et al., 2023). 
Specifically, in the next reversion, we will describe how to add new methods/problems to libmoon. If space is limited, we may relocate the empirical results to the appendix.

---
Reference

[1] Xin et al. Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help? NeurIPS 2022. 

[2] Hu et al. Revisiting Scalarization in Multi-Task Learning: A Theoretical Perspective. NeurIPS 2023. 

[3] Lin et al. Reasonable Effectiveness of Random Weighting: A Litmus Test for Multi-Task Learning. TMLR. 2022. 

[4] Liao et al. Does Continual Learning Meet Compositionality? New Benchmarks and An Evaluation Framework. NeurIPS DB/bench mark 2023.

[5] Sener et al. Multi-Task Learning as Multi-Objective Optimization. NeurIPS 2018.

Thank you for your responsible and careful checking for our submission. 

We had seriously checked the scope of the NeurIPS DB venue before our submission, and after careful investigation we believe our submission aligns with the NeurIPS DB scope, for the following reasons:

- **NeurIPS 2024 Guidance:** The NeurIPS 2024 scope includes "Benchmarks on new or existing datasets, as well as benchmarking tools" (6th bullet under the SCOPE section on their [website](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2024/CallForDatasetsBenchmarks)). Our work, which involves standardizing existing gradient-based multi-objective tools and testing problems, fits such demand.

- **Benchmark Tools:** The scope also includes benchmark testing tools (algorithms), not just problems. Our submission supports various synthetic and machine learning problems (e.g., ZDT, RE) and implements benchmarking algorithms like Smooth-Tche, MOO-SVGD, PMGDA, HVGrad, DirHV-EI, and PSL variants. These implementations span several categories, as shown in the table below:

**Table 1. New algorithms supported by Libmoon.**

| Method Type         | Previously in Matlab | Previously Unsupported (e.g., ML problems) | First Code Release                |
|---------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Tch-LCB, DirHV-EI   | ✔                    |                                            |                                   |
| MOO-SVGD, HVGrad    |                      | ✔                                          |                                   |
| Smooth-Tche, PMGDA, Evo-PSL |             |                                            | ✔                                 |

- **Beyond Software:** Libmoon provides full [source code](https://github.com/xzhang2523/libmoon), facilitating both industrial and academic development.

- **Precedents:** Examples like OpenML (Bischl et al 2021) and Bias Mitigation (Reddy et al 2021) also focus on supporting algorithms rather than just problems. And OpenML is also a software. 

> **Question. No new benchmark problems are introduced-only a gradient-based implementation of existing benchmarks**

This paper focus on benchmark methods (Table 3 in the main paper) rather than benchmark problems. As we have argued, benchmark methods also belong to benchmarks. 

---

Reference

[1] OpenML Benchmarking Suites. Bischl et al. NeurIPS DB. 2021. 

[2] Benchmarking Bias Mitigation Algorithms in Representation Learning through Fairness Metrics. Reddy et al. NeurIPS DB. 2021.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes a benchmark software suite for multi-objective optimization, including a number of problems which are implemented in a reasonably-comprehensive manner, with a focus on gradient-based algorithms.

review.value: This paper serves as the companion paper for the authors' multi-objective optimization suite. Overall, I am happy with the package, with detailed strengths and opportunities for improvement listed below.

strengths.value:
Multi-objective optimization is a **very important problem class**, and there is not enough work in the literature on it. From experience, many real-world problems are multi-objective, and the more serious the problem the more likely it is to need a formulation like this to correctly capture the engineering tradeoffs at play. A large part of my score is coming from this aspect alone.

Gradient-based methods are likewise very important, for the same reasons in multi-objective optimization as in ordinary optimization. Though I am less familiar with these techniques specifically since I don't work on these algorithms as part of my own research, the authors' choice seems reasonably comprehensive, and includes methods in several distinct classes of techniques so that users can find what they specifically need for their purposes.

It is good that the authors have included a review of other multi-objective optimization libraries, since this makes it much easier for readers looking for a benchmark library to identify what's out there. In situations where another one of the libraries is more applicable, for whatever reason, readers know where to find it.

I am also happy with the authors' technical description of different problem classes. I did not carefully check this due to time, but at short glance their review looks reasonable, and in any event there is standard material available which defines all of these notions. The authors include enough references that I have no doubt readers would be able to find it if needed.

Table 3 - which lists methods together with their solution properties, computational complexity, and other aspects - is very nice to have, since it helps readers choose which algorithm to try first, for instance as a comparison point.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Parts of the documentation are missing: for example, the "Overall Framework" section is empty. However, my impression from looking around is that pages like this are rare, so I'll overlook this element.

I am not aware of functionality which glues together the authors' package with BoTorch and other standard Bayesian optimization tooling. Indeed, their setup.py does not include BoTorch as a dependency, though the package is PyTorch-based. Bayesian optimization is a complex-enough algorithm class that it should not be implemented from scratch, due to a large set of details involving how to reliably handle the linear algebra which arises in posterior computations. Thus, including it in only a limited way is itself is a reasonable design choice: multi-objective Bayesian optimization should be handled by a proper Bayesian optimization library. **What I looked for, and did not find, was functionality that glues together the authors' package with BoTorch, so as to make multi-objective optimization algorithms built there easy to run on the authors' benchmark problems.** This would make a good addition to the package.

Finally, I would have preferred a backend-agnostic implementation so that at least the benchmark problems - even if not the baselines - are implemented in a way that also works in JAX (or even TensorFlow, for those who are still using it). However, I realize - having worked with a set of collaborators who have implemented a package that does this - that doing so is a non-trivial engineering challenge, and should not be viewed as a nice-to-have rather than a requirement.

**The font in the figures is unacceptably small, to the point of likely violating accessibility guidelines and I can't read any of it.** Please make the font substantially larger - at least 10-20x larger - the smallest font in the figures should be similar to the font used in the table which is directly above. In addition, please modify your color palette to account for red-green colorblindness.

limitations.value: In a benchmark library like this, the primary limitations I can see mainly concern comprehensiveness of implemented examples, which are detailed in the work.

correctness.value: I have no major concerns regarding correctness, everything looks reasonable.

clarity.value:
The paper is reasonably-well-written and I am overall happy with these aspects. The main thing I would change is to use a nicer-looking font in "Listing 1" and "Listing 2" (why are these called listings rather than figures?). The caption in Table 5 should also be at the bottom, putting caption on top is a very outdated style. Figure 5 should not occur between a small set of text that looks like it's part of Table 5's caption and should instead be moved to the bottom of the page.

Capitalization in the references is not handled correctly and needs to be fixed.

summary_and_contributions.value: This work introduces a library for gradient-based multi-objective optimization in Pytorch (LibMOON). The library attempts to encompass a big portion of MOO methods in ML (aggregation-based methods, gradient-modifiers methods, Pareto-set learning methods, as well as MOO Bayesian Optimization methods based on decomposition), a number of datasets (synthetic ones typically used in the evolutionary literature, as well as other baselines in the ML MOO literature), and a number of metrics to evaluate how well these methods capture the Pareto front in different aspects. Crucially, the library provides a simple interface to combine all the elements in the library (datasets, methods, solvers, and evaluation) in a few lines of code.

review.value: (intentionally left blank, as all the relevant fields are below)

strengths.value:
- It is indeed necessary for the community to have a common library where to implement all the methods and benchmarks, which is lacking at the moment.
- The library is quite ambitious in the number of types of methods that it encompasses.
- Besides more modern datasets, classical MOO synthetic problems are also considered in the library.
- The snippets of code are indeed quite short and simple, which can make testing the implement methods easy.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- For being a paper about a library, _I am missing key concepts being discussed in the paper_. For example, there is no discussion about how the code has been designed and implemented, and therefore it is really unclear: i) how easy/hard it is to add new methods or architectures; ii) how flexible is the code to add other solutions; or iii) the willingness/planning for the authors to keep the library activate and updated. As of now, it feels more as a black-box collection of static methods and benchmarks.

- What are reported as MTL problems are far from the typical settings tested in gradient-conflict MTL approaches (e.g., multi-MNIST, multi-classification in CelebA, NYUv2, Cityscapes, etc.).

- The empirical results do not serve much of a purpose in the current state of the manuscript, beyond assessing that the code works. It is a necessary sanity check, but I am not sure if they add much to the current paper.

limitations.value: The authors describe simple limitations of their work (extending to more models, dataset, etc.) but I don't think they discuss core limitations of their library (e.g., open-endedness, flexibility, API extensions, etc.) which are crucial for a library to be useful in the long term.

correctness.value: I assume experiments are properly conducted, but I have not checked all the code.

clarity.value: While the paper is generally well-written, it tries to explain too many concepts, and therefore it remains quite shallow in all of them. For example, as I am not familiar with MOBO/D methods, the text was insufficient for me to understand what they are about. Also, the taxonomy of methods and their names seems rather arbitrary and unconventional to me (e.g., agregation-based vs. SMOO methods).

relation_to_prior_work.value:
Again, since the paper touches so many sub-areas, it is hard to assess whether they relate with all prior work. As I am more familiar with MTL methods and gradient-conflict approaches, I think the paper falls quite short when it comes to this area.

For example, while the authors mention MGDA multiple times, they cite the work by Sener and Koltun, which proposed MGDA-UB, instead of the work by Desideri. Another area in which the work falls short, is that the authors do not mention the possibility of optimizing the last-common representation of the network (rather than $\theta$), which is precisely the contribution of the work of Sener and Koltun (i.e., applying MGDA to the shared feature $z$, rather than $\theta$). Moreover, there are no mentions to other works in gradient-conflict for MTL (e.g., [CAGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14048), [FAMO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03792), [RotoGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02631), or [PCGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06782), among others).

documentation.value:
Again, being a library paper, all the code is open-sourced and therefore technically available. However, I would expect a higher level of polish and _at least_ the existence of an actual documentation accompanying the code.

PS: I found that there are sphinx files in the repository, but they seem to be completely blank.

ethics.value: I don't think there are any concerns in this regard.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

- Figure 4 is way too small to read it.

title.value: A good attempt for gradient-based multi-objective optimization

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes the first framework for gradient-based multi-objective optimization: LibMOON. The proposed framework LibMOON can be used to evaluate gradient-based multi-objective solvers including discrete Pareto solution optimization, Pareto set learning, multi-objective Bayesian optimization. LibMOON includes those solvers, test problems and performance metrics. LibMOON can be used as a platform to design and evaluate new gradient-based multi-objective optimization algorithms.

review.value:
Pros:
1.	The proposed framework has high novelty and potentially high usefulness. This is because all of the well-known and frequently-used existing frameworks are for evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithms (whereas the proposed framework LibMOON is for gradient-based multi-objective optimization algorithms).
2.	It seems that the proposed framework is easy to use since it includes algorithms, test problems, and performance metrics.
3.	This paper is easy to read.

Cons:
1.	In the proposed framework in Fig. 1, it seems that pure multi-objective learning problems are not included whereas multi-task learning problems are included.
2.	In the abstract, the motivation of this paper is explained as follows: "Existing benchmark libraries for MOPs mainly  focus on evolutionary algorithms, most of which are zeroth-order methods that do not effectively utilize higher-order information from objectives and cannot scale to large-scale models with millions of parameters." However, high-scalability to large-scale models with millions of parameters is not discussed in detail.
3.	It seems that the supplementary file is incomplete. For example, in Lines 267-268, metrics are explained as follows: "The meaning of these metrics in Table 5 is left in Appendix A." However, in Appendix A, only subsection title "A.3 Metrics" is included with no explanations about each metrics.
4.	The ZDT1 test problem used in Section 5.2 “Pareto set learning” looks too simple. 
5.	In the EMO field, benchmarking is a hot research topic. That is, there exist a number of issues for performance comparison. There are no discussions about how to evaluate/compare trained Pareto set models in this paper.  
6.	In Fig. 1, available synthetic test problems are severely limited and/or biased.

strengths.value:
Strengths:
1.	The proposed framework has high novelty and potentially high usefulness.
2.	This paper is easy to read.

Weakness:
1.	No illustration related to the use of large-scale models with millions of parameters whereas the scalability is emphasized in the abstract as the motivation of this paper.
2.	Pure multi-objective learning problems are not included (whereas multi-task learning problems are included in the explanations in Fig. 1).
3.	There is no discussion about how to evaluate the trained Pareto set models.
4.	The supplementary file is incomplete.
5.	A test problem used in computational experiments looks too simple.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Line 27: "In non-degenerate problems, no single solution can attain the minimum of all objectives simultaneously."
In the EMO community, "degenerate problems" usually mean that the dimensionality of the Pareto front of an m-objective degenerate problem is less than (m - 1). Even in this case, no single solution can attain the minimum of all objectives simultaneously. Thus, it seems that this sentence may need some modifications. 

2. Lines 200-202: "LibMOONsupports three different network architecture to produce parameter"
English can be improved.

3. Line 280: "We use ZDT1 to illustrate the different behaviors of Pareto set learning (PSL) methods".
It seems that "ZDT1" is too simple for compare "Pareto Set Learning" methods. Fig. 4 simply explain the characteristic features of each scalarizing function.

title.value: Comments for "LibMOON: A Gradient-based MultiObjective OptimizatioN Library in PyTorch"

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper presents LibMOON, a comprehensive gradient-based multiobjective optimization library implemented in PyTorch. It addresses the gap in existing MOO libraries, which primarily support evolutionary algorithms, by offering state-of-the-art gradient-based methods that can scale to large models with millions of parameters. The library supports both synthetic and real-world problems, providing a fair benchmark and being open-sourced for the community.

review.value: Overall, the paper presents a valuable tool for the multiobjective optimization community.

strengths.value:
1. Novelty and Relevance: The introduction of a gradient-based MOO library is a significant advancement, filling a notable gap in the field. The focus on scalable solutions for large models is highly relevant given the current trends in machine learning.
2. Comprehensive Support for MOO Methods: By incorporating over twenty state-of-the-art gradient-based MOO methods, LibMOON offers a wide range of tools for researchers and practitioners. This comprehensive support is one of the paper's key strengths.
3. Ease of Use and Accessibility: The library's open-source nature and easy installation via pip make it accessible to a broad audience. This is crucial for encouraging adoption and fostering a community around the tool.
4. Empirical Validation: The paper provides empirical results demonstrating the effectiveness of LibMOON on various tasks, which helps validate the library's capabilities and performance.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Weaknesses and Areas for Improvement

1. Comparative Analysis: While the paper mentions existing libraries like pymoo, PlatEMO, and Pagmo, a more detailed comparative analysis of LibMOON against these libraries would strengthen the argument for its novelty and effectiveness. Including benchmarks or performance comparisons could provide more concrete evidence of LibMOON's advantages.
2. Usability and Documentation: Although the paper highlights the ease of installation, it would be beneficial to discuss the usability of the library in more detail. Are there comprehensive tutorials, documentation, and examples available to help new users get started? Including user feedback or case studies could also be valuable.
3. Scalability and Performance: The paper mentions GPU acceleration and scalability to large models but does not provide detailed benchmarks on performance scalability across different hardware configurations. Providing such benchmarks could help users understand the library's performance characteristics better.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
1. Introduction and Motivation: The introduction provides a good overview, but it could be enriched by explicitly stating the unique challenges that gradient-based MOO methods address compared to evolutionary algorithms. This would help readers understand the specific benefits of the approach taken by LibMOON.
2. Technical Details: The technical sections are well-detailed, but some parts could benefit from additional explanations or visual aids. For instance, diagrams illustrating the workflow of different gradient-based methods or comparisons of solution quality between different methods could be very informative.
3. Empirical Results: The empirical results are useful, but consider including more diverse datasets and problem types to demonstrate the library's versatility. Additionally, including a discussion on the trade-offs between different methods (e.g., accuracy vs. computational cost) would provide deeper insights.
4. User Engagement: Encouraging user contributions and feedback is essential for the growth of an open-source project. The paper could briefly mention how the community can contribute to LibMOON, report issues, or suggest improvements. Highlighting any ongoing collaborations or planned community events could also be beneficial.

TLDR.value: This paper introduces the first gradient based multiobjective optimization library

abstract.value: Multiobjective optimization problems (MOPs) are prevalent in machine learning, with applications in multi-task learning, learning under fairness or robustness constraints, etc. Instead of reducing multiple objective functions into a scalar objective, MOPs aim to optimize for the so-called Pareto optimality or Pareto set learning, which involves optimizing more than one objective function simultaneously, over models with thousands to millions of parameters. Existing benchmark libraries for MOPs mainly focus on evolutionary algorithms, most of which are zeroth-order or meta-heuristic methods that do not effectively utilize higher-order information from objectives and cannot scale to large-scale models with millions of parameters. In light of the above challenges, this paper introduces \algoname, the first multiobjective optimization library that supports state-of-the-art gradient-based methods, provides a fair and comprehensive benchmark, and is open-sourced for the community.

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
